ACTION:

Notice of availability.

SUMMARY:

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or the Agency) is announcing the issuance of four Emergency Use Authorizations (EUA or Authorization) under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for new animal products. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Elanco US Inc. for application on or around wounds for the prevention of infestations caused by New World screwworm (
Cochliomyia hominivorax ; NWS) larvae (myiasis) in sheep, cattle, goats, swine, camelids, and the following captive and captured wildlife species: cervids, American bison, bighorn sheep, and Sonoran pronghorn. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Zoetis Inc. for the treatment of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in dogs and puppies. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Bimeda Animal Health Ltd. for the prevention of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in cattle. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Sergeant's Pet Care Products LLC for the treatment and prevention of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in dogs, puppies, cats and kittens 2 pounds of body weight or greater and 4 weeks of age and older. The Authorizations contain, among other things, conditions on the emergency use of the authorized products. The Authorizations follow the August 18, 2025, determination by the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) that there is a significant potential for a public health emergency that has a significant potential to affect national security or the health and security of U.S. citizens living abroad and that involves NWS. On the basis of such determination, the Secretary of HHS declared on August 18, 2025, that circumstances exist justifying the authorization of emergency use of animal drugs to treat or prevent NWS myiasis in animals. The Authorizations, which include an explanation of the reasons for issuance, are reprinted in this document.

DATES:

The Authorizations are effective on their dates of issuance: August 7, 2026, August 13, 2026, August 27, 2026, and September 3, 2026, respectively.

ADDRESSES:

Submit written requests for single copies of the EUAs to the Policy and Regulations Staff, Center for Veterinary Medicine, Food and Drug Administration, 5001 Campus Drive, College Park, MD 20740. Send one self-addressed adhesive label to assist that office in processing your requests. See the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section for electronic access to the Authorizations.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Crystal Groesbeck, Center for Veterinary Medicine, Food and Drug Administration, 5001 Campus Drive, College Park, MD 20740, 240-402-0819,
Crystal.Groesbeck@fda.hhs.gov .

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background

Section 564 of the FD&C Act ( 21 U.S.C. 360bbb-3 ) allows FDA to strengthen public health protections against biological, chemical, nuclear, and radiological agents. Among other things, section 564 of the FD&C Act allows FDA to authorize the use of an unapproved medical product or an unapproved use of an approved medical product in certain situations. With this EUA authority, FDA can help ensure that medical countermeasures may be used in emergencies to diagnose, treat, or prevent serious or life-threatening diseases or conditions caused by biological, chemical, nuclear, or radiological agents when there are no adequate, approved, and available alternatives (among other criteria).

II. Criteria for EUA Authorization

Section 564(b)(1) of the FD&C Act provides that, before an EUA may be issued, the Secretary of HHS must declare that circumstances exist justifying the authorization based on one of the following grounds: (A) a determination by the Secretary of Homeland Security that there is a domestic emergency, or a significant potential for a domestic emergency, involving a heightened risk of attack with a biological, chemical, radiological, or nuclear agent or agents (CBRN); (B) a determination by the Secretary of Defense that there is a military emergency, or a significant potential for a military emergency, involving a heightened risk to U.S. military forces, including personnel operating under the authority of title 10 or title 50, U.S. Code, of attack with (i) a CBRN; or (ii) an agent or agents that may cause, or are otherwise associated with, an

( printed page 65563)

imminently life-threatening and specific risk to U.S. military forces; [ 1 ]

(C) a determination by the Secretary of HHS that there is a public health emergency, or a significant potential for a public health emergency, that affects, or has a significant potential to affect, national security or the health and security of U.S. citizens living abroad, and that involves a CBRN agent or agents, or a disease or condition that may be attributable to such agent or agents; or (D) the identification of a material threat by the Secretary of Homeland Security pursuant to section 319F-2 of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act ( 42 U.S.C. 247d-6b ) sufficient to affect national security or the health and security of U.S. citizens living abroad.

Once the Secretary of HHS has declared that circumstances exist justifying an authorization under section 564 of the FD&C Act, FDA may authorize the emergency use of a drug, device, or biological product if the Agency concludes that the statutory criteria are satisfied. Under section 564(h)(1) of the FD&C Act, FDA is required to publish in the
Federal Register
a notice of each authorization, and each termination or revocation of an authorization, and an explanation of the reasons for the action. Under section 564(h)(1) of the FD&C Act, revisions to an authorization shall be made available on FDA's website. Section 564 of the FD&C Act permits FDA to authorize the introduction into interstate commerce of a drug, device, or biological product intended for use in an actual or potential emergency when the Secretary of HHS has declared that circumstances exist justifying the authorization of emergency use. Products appropriate for emergency use may include products and uses that are not approved, cleared, or licensed under sections 505, 510(k), 512, or 515 of the FD&C Act ( 21 U.S.C. 355 , 360(k) , 360b , and 360e ) or section 351 of the PHS Act ( 42 U.S.C. 262 ), or conditionally approved under section 571 of the FD&C Act ( 21 U.S.C. 360ccc ).

Under section 564(c) of the FD&C Act, FDA may issue an EUA only if, after consultation with the HHS Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response, the Director of the National Institutes of Health, and the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (to the extent feasible and appropriate given the applicable circumstances), FDA [ 2 ]

concludes: (1) that an agent referred to in a declaration of emergency or threat can cause a serious or life-threatening disease or condition; (2) that, based on the totality of scientific evidence available to FDA, including data from adequate and well-controlled clinical trials, if available, it is reasonable to believe that: (A) the product may be effective in diagnosing, treating, or preventing (i) such disease or condition; or (ii) a serious or life-threatening disease or condition caused by a product authorized under section 564, approved or cleared under the FD&C Act, or licensed under section 351 of the PHS Act, for diagnosing, treating, or preventing such a disease or condition caused by such an agent; and (B) the known and potential benefits of the product, when used to diagnose, prevent, or treat such disease or condition, outweigh the known and potential risks of the product, taking into consideration the material threat posed by the agent or agents identified in a declaration under section 564(b)(1)(D) of the FD&C Act, if applicable; (3) that there is no adequate, approved, and available alternative to the product for diagnosing, preventing, or treating such disease or condition; (4) in the case of a determination described in section 564(b)(1)(B)(ii) of the FD&C Act, that the request for emergency use is made by the Secretary of Defense; and (5) that such other criteria as may be prescribed by regulation are satisfied. No other criteria for issuance have been prescribed by regulation under section 564(c)(4) of the FD&C Act.

Prioritizing Microservice Requests via Retries

Ofek Lavi 1
Jhonatan Tavori 4
Hanoch Levy 1
Anat Bremler-Barr 1

Affiliation: 1 Tel Aviv University 4 Columbia University

Abstract

Cloud services rapidly shift towards independently-managed microservices architectures. This independence may lead to temporary microservices miscoordination, resulting in overloads and rejections of valuable transactions. This weakness may further be exploited by attackers to launch overload attacks inflicting performance and cost damages.

Retry operations are a key machinery aiming at overcoming seldom rejections. However, during overload periods they: a) Fail protecting valuable transactions from rejections, and b) Trigger large-scale performance-degrading retry storms.

We propose simple modifications in retry operations, overcoming these deficiencies by transforming retries into a rejection prioritization mechanism, DiffTry (Differential Retries). It is based on a simple, lightweight, distributed and stateless design and requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination.

We develop an analytical model capturing DiffTry ’s effectiveness for two services in tandem, then generalize it to networks of services. Our theoretical framework lets practitioners quantify, for a given network, the resulting prioritization and rejection rates, and yields formal guarantees that DiffTry substantially reduces the impact of both incidental and adversarial orchestrated overloads. We validate these predictions in simulation and on a live Kubernetes deployment, where DiffTry is a simple drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application changes; the measured rejection closely matches the analysis.

I Introduction

Cloud service providers have largely converged on microservice architectures, decomposing monolithic applications into hundreds, often thousands, of loosely coupled services [ 1 , 2 ] .
This paradigm
allows each component
(microservice)
to scale elastically in response to demand,
implementing capacity scaling, retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers autonomously.

While these mechanisms achieve high microservice independence and simplicity in design, their coordination is challenging and their operations can get miscoordinated. During periods of miscoordination, in particular, miscoordination of service capacity, some microservices may become overloaded due to their service capacity not up-scaled to the load generated by upstream services. Such overload periods may result in significant losses of transactions, due to their blocking/rejection by the downstream overloaded microservice.

The negative economic effects of such rejection periods are further compounded when they affect high-value (high-priority) transactions. These may include premium transactions (such as a customer with a loaded cart, or a preferred customer), mission critical transactions and others.

Two main overload-prevention methodologies are used in the literature and in practice:
(i) local auto-scaling approaches (e.g., [ 3 ] ), and
(ii) network-wide centralized approaches (e.g., TopFull [ 4 ] , which offers network-wide source throttling).
Local auto-scaling reacts to overload by increasing resources at individual nodes. While it can respond quickly, it lacks a global view and therefore cannot address traffic miscoordination across services. Centralized approaches have such a global view, but require collecting network-wide information and are therefore slower to react. The resulting time gap can create temporary periods of miscoordination and overload, during which high-value transactions may still be rejected.
Malicious users can exploit this weakness by injecting spikes of cheap low-value transactions, overloading critical microservices and causing mass rejections of innocent high-value traffic, thereby inflicting economic damage on the service [ 5 ] .

In this paper, we propose DiffTry as a mechanism for service differentiation and load control using retries.

I-A DiffTry: Differential Retries

DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a simple and stateless mechanism for differential operation of retries across transaction classes, yielding differentiation (and prioritization) in their rejection rates.
In a nutshell, DiffTry intervenes right at the point where rejections occur, protecting high-priority transactions during overload by assigning class-specific retry limits.
The key idea is to assign a different number of retry attempt limits to different classes or tiers of requests. For example, a premium user may be allowed up to three attempts, while a ”bypassing user” may be limited to one. These limits can be configured per route, user tier or traffic class (e.g., with priority carried in an HTTP header), and enforced locally at the retry decision point (e.g., the sender API).

By embedding the prioritization logic directly into the retry process, DiffTry eliminates the need for explicit coordination or tight coupling between services. It effectively transforms retries into a distributed rejection-prioritization control, enabling systems to both prioritize critical flows and suppress retry amplification in a local, coordination-free, scalable manner.

During attacks, this may have a particularly critical effect, as it protects highly valued transactions from large volumes of attacking requests (naturally classified as low-priority tasks).
Furthermore, without requiring explicit overload detection or sensor, the mechanism has an effect only under high-load or overload conditions and remains effectively silent otherwise.

To illustrate DiffTry under overload, consider a front-end Service A and a downstream Service B (Fig. 1 ). Requests are labeled by priority, either High (e.g., premium or latency-sensitive users) or Low (e.g., a bypassing user or batch job), and Service A retries them after timeouts or errors.

((a))

((b))

Fig. 1 : DiffTry impact on retry behavior under overload.

In classical retry mechanisms (a), when Service B becomes overloaded due to a traffic spike or scaling lag, Service A retries failed requests, ignoring priority. Thus, transactions are rejected and delayed regardless of value. Although overload is often driven by low-priority traffic, and can be amplified by low-priority attack traffic, the main economic damage comes from degraded high-priority requests.
In contrast, with DiffTry (b), high-priority requests receive more retry attempts, increasing their success probability and reducing their rejection rate to around 15%. This selective persistence significantly improves their goodput : even when both classes contribute 50% of the input load, high-priority transactions account for about 85% of successful completions, corresponding to a throughput improvement of about 70%. This tradeoff can be further enhanced by adding retries to high-priority requests.

I-B Main Contributions: DiffTry Analysis and Results

Our paper focuses on establishing and analyzing the behavior of DiffTry . This should serve designers in (i) Gaining trust in this new machinery, (ii) Using the analysis to optimize the operations of DiffTry and plan the system
performance.

We start by presenting the DiffTry mechanism, properties, and model in Sec. III . Then,
we analyze a sub-system in which the upstream Service A sends traffic to the downstream Service B (Sec. IV ). We first focus on the overload region, and using a fluid-model approximation we derive the per-stream rejections and throughput.
We then consider the no-overload region, where rejection depends on the underlying queueing model. We show how queueing-specific blocking expressions can be plugged into our retry analysis, to derive the per-stream rejections; we demonstrate this on the M/M/1/m model.
Simulation results demonstrate the model accuracy in Sec. V .

Having established the analysis for a single overloaded node we turn to deal with networks (Sec. VI ).
This is motivated by real microservice systems, which often contain tens or hundreds of services, e.g., Uber [ 1 ] and Netflix [ 2 ] .
There are two key motivating questions behind this analysis: 1) Whether the plausible behavior (low rejections for high-priority transactions) derived for a single node would hold under an arbitrary network. In particular, could high-priority class enjoy low rejections in one node, but affect the traffic in a way that it will suffer high rejection rate on other (downstream) nodes. 2)
Approximate the network rejections under DiffTry .

We adopt the well known open-network model [ 6 ] , combined with flow classes/priorities, to model the traffic in the network. We then extend it to model DiffTry .
By incorporating the rejection equations we generate a set of equations whose solution
(computed in a simple iterative approach) yields the rejection rate of each priority class in each node. This allows deriving the end-to-end rejection rates.
We further prove that the iterative approach is always guaranteed to converge to a solution and derive network rejection probabilities.
We also investigate whether the solution is guaranteed to be unique (Sec. VI-E ).
We derive a set of conditions under which uniqueness is guaranteed. In particular it holds for a wide set of applications where the transaction flow graph is represented by a DAG (examples include Online Boutique [ 7 ] and WeChat [ 8 ] ). For other cases, we prove uniqueness for some cases, but the general theoretical problem remains open in the context of this work; for those cases, we conduct an extensive set of experiments, all of which yield a unique solution.

We establish monotonicity results (Sec. VI-G ) showing that network-wide class-level success rates increase monotonically with retry limits. This establishes the effectiveness of DiffTry as well as allowing establishing performance lower bounds.

Lastly, in Sec. VII we study DiffTry ’s network-level behavior
numerically and validate it on a live Kubernetes deployment.
There, DiffTry is a drop-in service-mesh plugin that needs no
application-code changes, and the measured rejection closely matches our
analysis, confirming that the local mechanism composes into network-wide
prioritization on a real system.
Concluding remarks are given in Sec. VIII .

II Related Work

Traffic and overload control are challenging in microservice systems due to miscoordination among independently auto-scaled services. Prior work shows that uncoordinated scaling decisions can lead to instability and excessive cost under burst workloads [ 9 , 10 ] .
Several recent studies address these challenges using centralized control. For example, [ 4 ] performs top-down overload control at the application ingress, [ 11 ] uses an application-wide controller to set global performance and resource targets, and [ 12 ] relies on centralized request routing and traffic engineering across services and replicas.

In cloud systems, retry mechanisms are tied to service communication protocols, including HTTP [ 13 ] and RPC [ 14 ] . Major cloud providers integrate automated retry logic directly into client and service libraries [ 15 , 16 ] , and service mesh platforms provide built-in retry handling at the infrastructure layer [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] ; all with a constant limit per route.

Traditional priority mechanisms (e.g., [ 6 ] ) are offered by cloud providers [ 21 , 22 ] , but their capabilities differ from DiffTry ’s. They attach the priority to the queue discipline , whereas DiffTry
attaches it to the retry budget . They were designed to prioritize transaction processing and are applied at the service point (of Service B, in Fig. 1 ), where transactions exit the queue and enter service, as opposed to DiffTry , which is applied before queue entrance, at the rejection point . As such, unless coordinated with other mechanisms, they would have difficulties handling rejections. Also, in no-overload situations, they may unnecessarily starve low-priority transactions and inflict long delays. An alternative approach, consisting of prioritization of rejections at the entrance to Service B, would be challenging to implement as well, since it would require coordination with the buffer management of Service B.

Recently, major cloud providers and service-mesh platforms have warned that retries can trigger retry storms and lead to performance problems and security threats [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] .
However, systematic analysis of retries under load remains limited, with only a small number of studies examining its impact on throughput and latency in microservice systems [ 26 , 19 ] .
DAGOR [ 8 ] also protects high-priority requests, but sheds at admission, requiring each server to sense overload and propagate its admission level upstream; RetryGuard [ 27 ] prevents retry storms, but without differentiating classes. DiffTry protects important jobs through the retry budget, needs neither overload detection nor coordination, and so acts immediately.

III DiffTry : Mechanism Operation and Model

As illustrated in Fig. 1 , the key idea of DiffTry is to assign different retry-attempt limits to requests from different priority classes.
By doing so, DiffTry ensures that high-priority requests receive preferential treatment under overload, while, at the same time, suppresses retry storms.
DiffTry is especially effective during miscoordination-induced overload periods and helps reduce the economic costs associated with it. It addresses three key problems in existing microservices applications:

1.

Insensitivity to priority: High-priority requests are rejected as much as low-priority ones.

2.

Retry amplification: Excessive retries inflate load and waste capacity and CPU.

3.

Over-scaling: Retried low-priority traffic triggers unnecessary scaling, increasing cost.

Background

Request To Clarify Why an Emergency AD Was Not Issued

Commenter #1 requested that the FAA clarify its determination that the unsafe condition does not meet the criteria for an emergency AD, given the potential interaction between fuel transfer systems, vibration-induced wear, and adjacent hydraulic and electrical components within the affected wing structure. Additionally, the commenter asked (1) if the low clearance condition could contribute to fuel starvation scenarios under certain operational conditions; (2) if interim inspections, operational limitations, or manufacturer service bulletins should be implemented while the rulemaking process proceeds; (3) if a shortened compliance period or immediate corrective action would better mitigate the identified risk; (4) if additional technical analysis regarding system interaction between fuel, hydraulic, and electrical components should be included in the final rulemaking record.

The FAA issues an emergency AD when an unsafe condition exists that requires immediate adoption, and the risk to the flying public justifies forgoing notice and comment prior to adopting an emergency AD. In developing this rulemaking, the FAA evaluated the compliance times and all the available information provided by Transport Canada and the manufacturer. The FAA has no additional data that would support reducing the compliance time below that specified in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49, or issuing an emergency AD to address the unsafe condition.

Further, the FAA provides the following additional information:

(1) The low clearance condition would not contribute to fuel starvation. There is no potential fouling condition of the fuel vent line and, therefore, no effect on the fuel system operation.

(2) The corrective actions and compliance times in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 are adequate for addressing the unsafe condition. Therefore, no interim actions, operational limitations, or additional service bulletins need to be mandated. However, operators are permitted to accomplish the requirements of this AD at an earlier time, or may voluntarily adopt service information, operational limitations, or additional inspections to address the unsafe condition.

(3) Neither a shorter compliance time nor immediate corrective action are necessary to address the unsafe condition. Based on the risk evaluation conducted by the manufacturer, the corrective actions and compliance times in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 are sufficient for mitigating the identified risk.

(4) There is no system failure associated with this unsafe condition; therefore, no technical analysis regarding system interaction between the fuel, hydraulic, and electrical components needs to be included in the rulemaking docket.

( printed page 65102)

Request To Reopen the Comment Period or Revise the Proposed AD

Commenter #2 requested that the FAA either (1) re-open the comment period and add to the AD docket all materials incorporated by reference and the basis for the cost assumptions and warranty offset, or (2) revise the proposed AD to add the operative standard and un-offset cost estimate. The commenter stated that the FAA did not provide adequate information for the public to meaningfully evaluate and comment on the proposed requirements and costs of compliance. The commenter further stated if the FAA cannot provide these elements, the proposed AD cannot be evaluated for comment or supported as a matter of reasoned decision-making and should be withdrawn and reissued with a complete record.

The FAA disagrees with the requests. The FAA provides summaries and access details in the preamble and regulatory text, makes materials available for inspection at FAA and National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) offices, offers publisher contact information, and obtains formal incorporation by reference (IBR) approval from the Office of the Federal Register. These efforts are intended to ensure that all IBR materials meet the “reasonably available” standard required by 1 CFR part 51 . The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.

Further, the FAA notes that this AD incorporates by reference Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49, not the manufacturer service information referenced in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 (
i.e.,
non-IBR material). The FAA posted Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 to the AD docket when the NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
. The non-IBR material may only be posted before the final rule's publication if it is already publicly available or if there is written consent from the owner of that material. Additionally, affected operators that must comply with the AD may obtain the non-IBR material directly from the manufacturer during the comment period through their normal course of business.

Further, the FAA based the estimated Costs of Compliance with this AD on information provided by the manufacturer. The number of estimated work hours and warranty terms are included in the manufacturer service bulletin, which is posted to the rulemaking docket upon publication of the final rule. The estimated parts cost was provided by the manufacturer. The FAA notes that no comments were received regarding the IBR material or estimated costs from any of the affected operators.

Conclusion

These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.

AGENCY:

Office of Personnel Management.

ACTION:

Direct final rule.

SUMMARY:

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to OPM's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations to incorporate various statutory amendments. The rule reflects statutory changes making virtually all Federal civilian service and certain honorable active military service qualify for determining FMLA eligibility, making clear that annual and sick leave provided under an authority outside of title 5, United States Code, may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave, and excluding certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees from title 5 FMLA coverage.

DATES:

This rule is effective December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026. If significant adverse comments are received, OPM will withdraw the affected provisions of this rule and issue a notice of proposed rulemaking.

ADDRESSES:

You may submit comments for this direct final rule within the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov/​ .
Follow the instructions for submitting comments.

All comments must be received by the end of the comment period for them to be considered. All comments and other submissions received generally will be posted on the internet at
regulations.gov
as they are received, without change, including any personal information provided. However, OPM retains discretion to redact personal or sensitive information, including but not limited to personal or sensitive information pertaining to third parties.

A summary of this rule may be found in the docket for this rulemaking at
www.regulations.gov .

Julie Ohr, Office of Personnel Management, Workforce Policy and Innovation, (202) 606-2858,
leavepolicy@opm.gov .

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

This direct final rule amends OPM's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations in subpart L of part 630 of title 5, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) to reflect statutory changes enacted in January 2021 [ 1 ]

and December 2023. [ 2 ]

I. Background and Effect on Paid Parental Leave

The Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993, as amended, provides eligible employees with unpaid, job-protected leave for specified family and medical reasons under one of two separate and independent authorities, known as title I and title II of the FMLA. Title II of the FMLA added a Family and Medical Leave subchapter V in chapter 63 of title 5 of the United States Code ( 5 U.S.C. chapter 63 , subchapter V), so it is generally referred to as “title 5 FMLA.” Title 5 FMLA is administered by OPM and applies to most Federal employees who are covered by the Federal leave system under 5 U.S.C. chapter 63 and some additional categories of employees. Title I of FMLA (non-title 5 FMLA), administered by the Department of Labor (DOL), applies to private sector employees, State and local Government employees, as well as some Federal employees (including employees of the U.S. Postal Service and the Postal Regulatory Commission). DOL's FMLA regulations are found in 29 CFR part 825 and should not be applied to employees covered by title 5 FMLA.

The 2021 and 2023 statutory amendments to the title 5 FMLA law also affect an employee's eligibility for paid parental leave (PPL). This is because PPL is a type of paid leave that is substituted for unpaid FMLA leave. Therefore, to be eligible for PPL, an employee must meet all eligibility requirements for use of FMLA leave as a covered “employee” (as defined in 5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(A) ) who has completed at least 12 months of qualifying service (as required by 5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(B) ). On August 10, 2020, OPM issued interim final FMLA/PPL regulations ( 85 FR 48075 ) to implement the Federal Employee Paid Leave Act (FEPLA), [ 3 ]

which authorizes the substitution of up to 12 weeks of PPL for unpaid FMLA leave granted in connection with the birth of an employee's son or daughter or the placement of a son or daughter with an employee for adoption or foster care. (See 5 U.S.C. 6382(a)(1)(A) and (B) .) To implement FEPLA, OPM added new regulatory subpart Q (Paid Parental Leave) in 5 CFR part 630 and made necessary clarifications, changes, and additions in subpart L (Family and Medical Leave). Because the 2021 and 2023 statutory amendments addressed in this rule affect FMLA eligibility, those amendments (and this rule) therefore also affect PPL eligibility.

The 2021 and 2023 statutory amendments to title 5 FMLA were enacted after the publication of OPM's interim final FMLA/PPL rule and have been implemented through policy guidance in two OPM memoranda to heads of agencies titled “Technical Amendments Related to Family and Medical Leave and Paid Parental Leave under Section 1103 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021” (CPM 2021-07, January 14, 2021) [ 4 ]

and “Amendment Related to Inclusion of Certain Military Active Service for Family and Medical Leave and Paid Parental Leave Eligibility Purposes under Section 1114 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024” (CPM 2024-05, February 13, 2024). [ 5 ]

The changes made in this direct final rule implement clear statutory requirements and codify the guidance found in those memoranda.

( printed page 65438)

II. January 2021 Statutory Amendments and Corresponding Regulatory Changes

The January 2021 amendments [ 6 ]

to the FMLA law revised 5 U.S.C. 6301(2)(v) , 5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(B) and 5 U.S.C. 6382(d)(1) and (2) and became effective on the date of the enactment of Public Law 116-283 , January 1, 2021. This section further explains each amendment and the corresponding regulatory changes.

1. The statutory amendment to section 6301(2)(v) changed the scope of employees excluded from coverage under the title 5 FMLA law. Before the amendment, section 6301(2)(v) provided that VHA physicians, dentists, and nurses in the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) were excluded from the title 5 annual and sick leave system, since they were covered by a leave system established under 38 U.S.C. 7421 . However, the original title 5 FMLA law definition of “employee” ( 5 U.S.C. 6381(1) ) expressly included these employees as covered by title 5 FMLA. While these employees were covered by the title 5 FMLA law, OPM's FMLA regulations provided that they would be covered by FMLA regulations prescribed by the VA Secretary (see 5 CFR 630.1201(b)(3)(i) and (4) ), which were required to be consistent with the OPM regulations. The amended title 5 FMLA law, currently in effect, excludes all VHA employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from coverage under the title 5 FMLA law. These employees are governed by a FMLA law in 38 U.S.C. 7425(c) , which requires that VA provide family and medical leave in the same manner and subject to the same limitations to the maximum extent practicable, as family and medical leave is provided under the title 5 FMLA law.

To conform with the January 2021 amendments to sections 6301(2)(v) and 6381(1) OPM is removing 5 CFR 630.1201(b)(3)(i) dealing with VHA employees listed in 38 U.S.C. 7401(1) and covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 , since paragraph (b)(3) concerns employees covered by the title 5 FMLA law. OPM is also amending paragraph (b)(4), which connects to paragraph (b)(3), to remove the reference to the VA Secretary. OPM is redesignating the remaining paragraphs (b)(3)(ii) and (iii) as paragraphs (b)(3)(i) and (ii). OPM is adding a new paragraph (v) in § 630.1201(b)(2), which lists positions to which the subpart L FMLA regulations do not apply. Paragraph (b)(2)(v) provides that subpart L does not apply to all VHA employees covered by a leave system established under 38 U.S.C. 7421 .

2. The statutory amendment to section 6381(1)(B) broadened FMLA coverage by making virtually all types of civilian Federal service (including employment on a temporary or intermittent basis) qualifying service for purposes of applying the FMLA eligibility requirement of 12 months of qualifying service. Before the amendment, the 12 months of service must have been as an “employee” who was covered by the title 5 FMLA leave provisions (as described in 5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(A) )—that is, serving in a position in which the employee was eligible to use FMLA leave under the title 5 FMLA law. The amended law, currently in effect, requires that an employee complete at least 12 months of service as an employee (as defined in 5 U.S.C. 2105 ) of the Government of the United States, including service with the United States Postal Service, the Postal Regulatory Commission, or a non-appropriated fund instrumentality (NAFI) as described in section 2105(c). Thus, virtually all types of civilian Federal service (including employment on a temporary or intermittent basis) are now qualifying for purposes of applying the FMLA eligibility requirement for 12 months of qualifying service. (To be eligible to use title 5 FMLA leave, an employee must still meet the definition of “employee” in 5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(A) . For example, those currently employed on a temporary or intermittent basis remain ineligible to use title 5 FMLA leave.)

To conform with the amendment to section 6381(1)(B), OPM is revising 5 CFR 630.1201(b)(1)(ii)(A) to codify that service as an employee under 5 U.S.C. 2105 is qualifying for purposes of applying the FMLA eligibility requirement for 12 months of qualifying service. Qualifying service includes service by employees serving on a temporary or intermittent basis who meet the definition of “employee” in 5 U.S.C. 2105 .

OPM is also adding a paragraph (G) in § 630.1201(b)(1)(ii) to address that service with the United States Postal Service or the Postal Regulatory Commission is qualifying service. There is an existing paragraph (D) in § 630.1201(b)(1)(ii) providing that service by a NAFI employee under 5 U.S.C. 2105(c) is qualifying service. While section 6381(1)(B) did not address such NAFI service before the 2021 statutory amendments, the treatment of NAFI employees under the title 5 FMLA law (including the creditability of NAFI service towards the 12-month service requirement) was already addressed in 5 U.S.C. 2105(c)(1)(E) and in OPM FMLA regulations back to 1993. [ 7 ]

3. The statutory amendments to section 6382(d)(1) and (2) made clear that an employee may substitute annual or sick leave earned under an authority outside of title 5, United States Code, for unpaid FMLA leave by removing the requirement that the annual or sick leave be under the leave system established under 5 U.S.C. chapter 63 , subchapter I. The law in effect before the amendment only addressed the substitution of annual or sick leave credited “under subchapter I.” The amended law, currently in effect, clarifies that the rules governing the substitution of annual or sick leave for unpaid FMLA leave apply equally to annual or sick leave provided under a non-title 5 authority.

No revision to the regulations governing the substitution of paid leave is necessary because § 630.1206(b)(2)(i) and (c)(1) already allow annual or sick leave under an “equivalent annual or sick leave under another authority” to be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave.

III. December 2023 Statutory Amendment and Corresponding Regulatory Change

The December 2023 technical amendment [ 8 ]

to the title 5 FMLA law revised 5 U.S.C. 6381(1)(B) to allow qualifying military service to count toward the 12-month service requirement for FMLA eligibility. That amendment became effective on the date of the enactment of Public Law 118-31 , December 22, 2023. This section further explains the amendment and the corresponding regulatory change.

The statutory amendment to section 6381(1)(B) broadened FMLA eligibility by providing that service “which qualifies as honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps of the United States” is qualifying service for the purpose of establishing eligibility for title 5 FMLA leave (and for paid parental leave for employees who otherwise qualify based on the birth or placement of a child). The law in effect before the 2023 amendment required completion of at least 12 months of service “as an employee (as defined in section 2105) of the Government of the United States, including service with the United States Postal Service, the Postal Regulatory Commission, and a nonappropriated

( printed page 65439)

fund instrumentality as described in section 2105(c).” Section 2105 refers to civilian employees appointed in the civil service. Thus, service with an armed force was not qualifying service (other than service qualifying under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act or otherwise performed during an interruption in Federal civilian service as described in 5 CFR 630.1201(b)(1)(ii)(F) ). The amended law, currently in effect, allows honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps of the United States to count towards the 12-month service requirement for establishing eligibility for title 5 FMLA leave (and for paid parental leave for employees who otherwise qualify based on the birth or placement of a child). Thus, an employee may meet the 12-month service requirement for title 5 FMLA leave eligibility purposes through any combination of qualifying civilian service and qualifying military service. Based on the law, qualifying military service does not include service in the Coast Guard or in the commissioned corps of the Public Health Service.

OPM is revising 5 CFR 630.1201(b)(1)(ii) by adding a new paragraph (H), which addresses qualifying military service. This revision conforms to the current statute, as explained below.
